tier_reason: Upgraded from C: the CGAL comparison code is public (tests/benchmark/asymptotic/*.cpp for pgl, tests/benchmark/asymptotic/baseline/*.cpp for CGAL 6.1.2), doc/cgal.md states g++ -std=c++23 -O2 -DNDEBUG, and the linked data repo gfonsecabr/pgl-benchmarks records the CPU models (AMD Ryzen 9 9900X, Intel Xeon w5-3433) and GCC 16.2.1 in each machine's CGAL baseline file. Every table ratio in the record matches doc/cgal.md.

corrections.hardware: Two machines, one run each: AMD Ryzen 9 9900X 12-Core Processor and Intel Xeon w5-3433 (named in the meta block of gfonsecabr/pgl-benchmarks history/asymptotic-baseline/*.json; doc/cgal.md itself does not name them). Ratios are per-machine pgl/CGAL, then averaged over the two machines.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Ratios are pgl time / CGAL time (below 1 = pgl faster), median over input sizes, range in parentheses, averaged over two machines. ERational vs EPECK, pgl faster: regularized union of triangles 0.23x (0.20-0.59), arrangement point-location query 0.46x (0.32-0.84), segment intersection 0.55x (0.19-1.8), arrangement point-location build 0.61x (0.46-0.87), segment search count in Rectangle 0.68x (0.55-0.91); near parity: nearest-neighbour query 0.82x (0.63-1.1), kd-tree build 0.88x (0.63-1.4), visibility 0.90x, two-polygon union 0.93x. int vs EPICK, pgl faster: point search count in Triangle 0.21x and segment search count in Triangle 0.21x, segment intersection 0.35x (CGAL's EPICK sweep is not exact; pgl's exact int version is 0.20x against EPECK), segment search count in Rectangle 0.51x, convex hull 0.51x, visibility 0.73x. CGAL faster: Delaunay triangulation (pgl 2.6x slower ERational/EPECK, 1.7x slower int/EPICK), point search count in Triangle with ERational (2.4x), convex hull with ERational (1.8x), Minkowski sum (1.7x), triangulation point location with ERational (1.7x), and with int/EPICK the kd-tree build (1.7x), nearest-neighbour query (1.8x), segment search build (1.8x) and triangulation point-location build (1.4x). Overall ERational/EPECK spans CGAL 2.6x faster to pgl 4.4x faster; int/EPICK spans CGAL 1.8x faster to pgl 4.8x faster.
corrections.caveats: First-party comparison, but fully reproducible (code, compiler, flags and CPU models public), so tier A. doc/cgal.md says pgl is tuned against this very benchmark, so the comparison favours pgl. Some rows favour pgl by construction: CGAL Kd_tree has no triangle query, so the benchmark wrote one for the 'count in Triangle' rows, which is where pgl's int column looks best; CGAL's Range_tree_2 is deliberately not run. Mixed result: CGAL wins Delaunay triangulation, Minkowski sum, triangulation point location, and with int/EPICK the kd-tree build and nearest-neighbour query. Ratios are averaged over two machines, one run each. The table changes often (it was refreshed 2026-09-23 and re-averaged 2026-09-26), so re-read before quoting. Very young project (6 stars). Do not read it as a blanket CGAL replacement.

notes: Every ratio quoted in the record matches the doc/cgal.md table; I only added rows it left out (for example CGAL 1.8x faster on the int/EPICK nearest-neighbour query, which the record listed as a pgl win under ERational only). Upgraded to A after finding the CPU models in the linked data repo. The dashboard at gfonsecabr.github.io is blocked from this container. tier_reason: The author's phtree-cpp-perf repo has public benchmark code and raw Google Benchmark output against Boost.Geometry's R-tree, and the insert and window-query figures in the record match the result files. The CPU model is never named ('8 X 4600 MHz', 12 MiB L3), so this is first-party C, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Insert at 1M entries (CUBE / CLUSTER): points PhTreeMM 2.79M/s vs BoostRT 500k/s and 3.97M/s vs 781k/s (about 5.6x and 5.1x, derived from page data); boxes PhTree3D 1.44M/s vs BoostRT 406k/s and 3.18M/s vs 573k/s (about 3.5x and 5.6x, derived); libspatialindex is slower still. Window queries are mixed: point data at 1M, PhTree3D 314k q/s vs BoostRT 364k q/s on CUBE (Boost 1.16x faster) and 1.35M q/s vs 990k q/s on CLUSTER (PH-tree 1.36x faster), with about 3-4 results per query; with about 100 results per query BoostRT wins (121k vs 84k q/s for PhTreeMM2 on CUBE). Box data at 1M on CUBE: PhTree3D 56.3k q/s vs BoostRT 263.6k q/s (Boost about 4.7x faster). kNN clearly favours Boost: 3D, 1M points, k=1, BoostRT 736k/741k q/s vs PhTree3D 28.4k/54.9k q/s on CUBE/CLUSTER (Boost about 26x and 13x faster, derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 12.1 (insert and window-query runs, 2023-02-01/02) and Clang 14.0.0 (3D kNN run, 2023-03-09; the 10D block is labelled 'GCC 14.0.0'). Built with bazel --config=benchmark, which in the current .bazelrc means opt mode with -O3 -g -mavx -mbmi2 -std=c++17. The result files do not record the flags used at the time.
corrections.caveats: Benchmark written and run by the PH-tree author in a separate repo (tzaeschke/phtree-cpp-perf, MIT, 0 stars). The phtree-cpp README does not link to it, and it vendors PH-tree C++ 1.4.0, while the library is now at 1.7.0. Results date from February-March 2023. The perf README notes that Boost RT was driven with std::array coordinates (a small slowdown), that the libspatialindex wrapper uses a buffering hack, and that an unexplained libspatialindex bug appears on the WEB dataset. The win is insertion (about 5x over Boost's R-tree). Window queries are mixed and box queries favour Boost; 3D kNN favours Boost by about 13-26x. CPU model not named (8 x 4600 MHz, 12 MiB L3), so not tier A. Fork of Improbable's unmaintained original, now maintained by the original PH-tree developer.

notes: Numbers checked line by line in results_insert_mm_d.txt, results_insert_mm_box_d.txt, results_query_mm_d.txt, results_query_mm_box_d.txt and results_knn_mm_d.txt. The record understated how badly PH-tree loses kNN to Boost, so I added the figures. tier_reason: README gives the 1.46x/4.14x/1.25x vs nanoflann and 1.73x/1.8x/3.21x vs OpenCV FLANN figures with no hardware, compiler, flags, k or code for the nanoflann comparison; the repo's testperformance.cpp (added 2026-04-27) races only OpenCV FLANN, so first-party C.

corrections.caveats: First-party README numbers (2018) with no hardware, compiler, flags or k stated, and an internal inconsistency (heading says 10,000 2D points, block says 'Speed up in 3D points'). The repo has no nanoflann benchmark code: testperformance.cpp (added 2026-04-27, -O3 -march=native, KNN=10, 1,000 queries) compares picoflann v1/v2 only against OpenCV FLANN. An independent but small benchmark (LimHyungTae/OpenFLANN, 18 stars, PCL wrappers, 1,000 repeats, no hardware stated; numbers in its imgs/knn_*.png tables) found nanoflann faster at small K: 10,000 points K=1 0.00104 ms vs 0.00149 ms and K=10 0.00213 vs 0.00358 ms; 200,000 points K=1 0.00215 vs 0.00242 ms. Picoflann is much faster only at large K (200,000 points, K=5000: 0.84 ms vs 8.36 ms). Its author concludes 'For robotics application, NanoFLANN is better'. So the 4.14x knn figure does not hold at the small K most users need. No LICENSE file (LICENSE, LICENSE.txt, LICENSE.md, COPYING all 404) and no licence header in picoflann.h, so reference only. nanoflann is not a listed incumbent here.

notes: README numbers match the record. I confirmed the independent OpenFLANN figures in the record's caveats from its knn_1.png and knn_3.png tables and added the 10,000-point rows. Metadata checked on github.com: 22 stars, no license, not a fork, last commit 2026-04-27 (active).
